name: Galápagos Islands
blurb: Cold upwelling feeds sea lions, penguins and seaweed-eating iguanas.

tip.title: Switch off the upwelling
tip.text: In El Niño years the cold, nutrient-rich current stops rising near the islands. Cut Cold upwelling and watch algae, sardines, iguanas, penguins and sea lions.

notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae that bloom where cold, nutrient-rich water is pushed up around the islands. They feed the zooplankton and small fish that the marine food web rests on.

nodes.name: Intertidal algae
nodes.desc: Red and green seaweeds grow on the rocky shore in the cold, nutrient-rich water. Marine iguanas and crabs graze them.

nodes.name: Prickly pear cactus
nodes.desc: Cactus whose pads, flowers and fruit feed tortoises and finches. On some islands it grows tree-like, which keeps its pads out of reach of grazers.

nodes.name: Grasses
nodes.desc: Grasses and low plants of the arid lowlands and the wetter highlands. Tortoises, finches and introduced goats graze them.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting grazers that eat phytoplankton and are in turn eaten by small schooling fish.

nodes.name: Sardines and small schooling fish
nodes.desc: Small schooling fish eating plankton. Sea lions, penguins and cormorants hunt them, and they die off or move away in El Niño years.

nodes.name: Sally Lightfoot crab
nodes.desc: Bright red crab on the lava shore. It mainly grazes algae but is an opportunist that also eats animal matter and scavenges dead seals and birds.

nodes.name: Marine iguana
nodes.desc: The only sea-going lizard. It feeds almost entirely on red and green seaweed, and populations crash when El Niño kills off its algae.

nodes.name: Darwin's finches
nodes.desc: A group of closely related finches whose beaks fit different foods. Some eat cactus fruit, flowers and buds, others seeds and insects.

nodes.name: Galápagos giant tortoise
nodes.desc: A huge herbivore that eats cactus, grasses, leaves and lichens and gets much of its water from Opuntia and dew. Long-lived adults have no natural predators.

nodes.name: Feral goat (introduced)
nodes.desc: Introduced goats strip vegetation and compete with tortoises for grazing. They were removed from Santiago by 2006.

nodes.name: Flightless cormorant
nodes.desc: A flightless bird that hunts fish and small octopuses in shallow water near shore. A 1983 El Niño cut its numbers by about half.

nodes.name: Galápagos penguin
nodes.desc: The only penguin living on the equator. It depends on cold Cromwell Current upwelling to supply the small fish it eats.

nodes.name: Galápagos sea lion
nodes.desc: Eats mainly sardines plus squid, octopus and crustaceans. Sharks hunt it, and its numbers fall when El Niño drives away its prey.

nodes.name: Black rat (introduced)
nodes.desc: Introduced omnivore that eats eggs and hatchlings of tortoises and iguanas and has wiped out young tortoises on some islands.

nodes.name: Scalloped hammerhead
nodes.desc: A schooling shark that eats mainly bony fish, along with squid and octopus. It is an opportunist that takes what is abundant.

nodes.name: Galápagos shark
nodes.desc: A large reef shark of the islands. It eats fish and is among the sharks that hunt sea lions and occasionally marine iguanas.

nodes.name: Galápagos hawk
nodes.desc: The islands' top land predator. It eats insects, lizards, rodents, small birds and young iguanas and tortoises, and scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Equatorial sunlight powers algae at sea and desert plants on land.

nodes.name: Cold upwelling
nodes.desc: Seamounts push the nutrient-rich Cromwell Current upward near the islands. El Niño shuts this upwelling off and warms the water.

nodes.name: Seasonal rain and mist
nodes.desc: The cold current brings drizzle for much of the year, and rainfall swings wildly between years, with El Niño years much wetter.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to soil and sea.

link_ideas.what: Cromwell Current upwelling and El Niño links Galapagos productivity to the wider equatorial Pacific
